newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: S.Lanka opposition says to wait on election reform.
newsitem.headline: S.Lanka opposition says to wait on election reform.

text.p: Sri Lanka's main opposition party decided on Monday to wait until the government came up with its final version of proposed amendments to the country's election system before indicating whether or not it gave its support.

The meeting of United National Party (UNP) lawmakers on Monday had been closely watched for signs of the party's thinking on government plans to change the constitution, a major thrust of which is devolution for ethnic minorities aimed at ending a protracted war.
UNP officials said the government had been flip-flopping on the election proposals and added it was better to wait until it had made its mind on what it had to offer.
The UNP decision to wait could interfere with government hopes of implementing the reforms quickly.

The ruling People's Alliance government, which has a single seat majority in the 225 seat parliament, requires the support of the UNP to get a two-thirds majority vote in parliament to pass the new constitution.
UNP has 94 seats in parliament but influences other smaller parties.
The government has said it will present its constitutional reform package in parliament ahead of the November budget session.

It is proposing to convert the current proportional representation election system into a hybrid of proportional representation and first-past-the-post, where each voter casts only one vote and the candidate receiving the most votes is the winner.

Political analysts have said the proposed new system would ensure fair representation, especially for minorities, and is necessary for the success of government's devolution package that aims to turn Sri Lanka into a federal state in all but name, granting some autonomy to minority Tamils.
Government troops have fought a war since 1983 against Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam rebels who demand a separate homeland for minority Tamils in Sri Lanka's north and east.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war. The LTTE put the toll higher.

UNP officials said party lawmakers also opposed the idea of a referendum on the draft constitution, saying the government should abide by the present constitutional requirement for a two-third parliamentary majority to approve the changes.

But the constitution also empowers President Chandrika Kumaratunga to call referendums on major national issues, and the ruling People's Alliance has said it will go to the people if UNP support on constitutional reforms is not forthcoming.
